paragraphs: This paper introduces boundary thickness as a way to understand a classifier’s robustness. The central question is how the structure of the region separating predictions relates to performance under changed or corrupted inputs. The authors connect thicker boundaries with better robustness and thinner boundaries with overfitting, including a larger gap between robust performance on training and test data.

They examine both adversarial examples and transformations that move inputs outside the training distribution. Their results show that increasing boundary thickness can improve robustness in these settings, including the robust test accuracy of adversarial training. They also find that several familiar regularization and data augmentation procedures can increase thickness, providing a shared perspective on methods usually discussed separately.

The theoretical analysis connects maximizing boundary thickness during training with mixup training. Building on that connection, the authors add noise augmentation to mixup and show further increases in thickness alongside improved resistance to attacks and distribution changes. They also identify thicker boundaries accompanying improvements in several existing approaches.
neurips-2020-boundary-thickness-and-robu.tldr: Boundary thickness connects classifier geometry with robustness and motivates adding noise augmentation to mixup training.

paragraphs: In structured bandit problems, a learner chooses among actions while learning about their rewards. This paper asks whether an algorithm can achieve strong long-run regret guarantees while also keeping regret bounded on instances where that is possible. Existing asymptotically optimal methods use forced sampling, which introduces regret that continues growing even on such easier instances.

For a finite set of hypotheses, the authors introduce CROP. It uses a pessimistic hypothesis to identify informative actions whose outcomes can eliminate optimistic hypotheses. This mechanism removes the need for forced exploration. The finite-time analysis establishes asymptotic optimality up to a constant factor, adaptation to bounded regret, and a bound governed by an effective number of actions rather than the total number.

The paper also describes a problem class where CROP can improve exponentially over existing algorithms before the asymptotic regime. In that class, even an oracle following an asymptotically optimal sampling scheme can incur linear worst-case regret. The finding highlights why long-run optimality alone may poorly describe finite-time behavior.
neurips-2020-crush-optimism-with-pessimi.tldr: CROP combines constant-factor asymptotic optimality with bounded-regret adaptation for structured bandits with finitely many hypotheses.

paragraphs: Recording many neurons across several brain areas creates an interpretation problem: individual neurons can mix signals associated with different task variables. Consequently, activity shared between regions can be difficult to connect to a particular aspect of behavior. This paper develops demixed shared component analysis, or dSCA, to separate task-related variables while examining what different regions share.

The method compresses population activity into a small set of components. Those components are constructed to capture as much shared information across brain areas as possible while retaining dependence on relevant task parameters. This gives the resulting representation two linked meanings: which task variables are shared between regions, and when that sharing appears over time.

The authors illustrate dSCA by reanalyzing two datasets from decision-making tasks in rodents and macaques. They report new insights into shared computation associated with several aspects of decision formation. The contribution is an interpretable analysis of coordinated population activity that keeps task identity and timing visible, rather than leaving them mixed together in individual neural responses.
neurips-2020-demixed-shared-component-an.tldr: dSCA separates task-related signals to reveal what information brain areas share and when they share it.

paragraphs: Feature interactions describe situations where inputs jointly influence a model’s behavior. Detecting those relationships can reveal structure that examining each input separately would miss. This paper studies how interactions learned by a trained neural network can be extracted by examining the network’s connectivity, using an observation about interacting features having strong connections to common hidden units.

The authors turn this connectivity perspective into a measure of interaction strength based on persistent homology, a theory for analyzing topological structure. They then develop the Persistence Interaction Detection algorithm, or PID, around that measure. The approach treats the network’s weighted connections as evidence about relationships among inputs, linking an interaction detection procedure to the organization of the trained model.

PID is evaluated on multiple interaction detection tasks using synthetic and real-world datasets, with different hyperparameter choices. The reported experiments show better performance than the state-of-the-art baselines used in those evaluations. These findings support topological analysis as an effective way to recover learned interactions from networks across the tested settings.
neurips-2020-detecting-interactions-from.tldr: PID uses a persistent-homology measure of neural-network connectivity to detect learned feature interactions.

paragraphs: Learning a graphical model becomes difficult when some of its variables are hidden. This paper studies Restricted Boltzmann Machines, a prominent family of such latent-variable models, by connecting their learnability to that of two-layer neural networks. The connection lets the authors address two learning problems through a common theoretical framework.

For the neural-network side, inputs are bounded in the infinity norm, meaning that their individual coordinates are bounded. The authors obtain nearly optimal results for both problems under a conjecture about the computational difficulty of sparse parity with noise. That qualification matters: the claimed near-optimality is tied to the stated hardness conjecture, rather than being an unconditional characterization.

The paper also begins a theoretical study of supervised Restricted Boltzmann Machines. Here, the underlying graphical model supplies distributional assumptions linked to the architecture of the function being learned. For a natural class of these models, the authors give an algorithm with better runtime than is possible for the related network class without those assumptions. This shows how distributional structure can change computational learnability.
neurips-2020-from-boltzmann-machines-to-.tldr: Connections between Restricted Boltzmann Machines and two-layer networks yield learning guarantees and show how distributional assumptions can improve runtime.

paragraphs: Given a collection of three-dimensional parts that form one object, an assembly system must determine where each part belongs and how it should be oriented. This paper addresses that visual pose estimation problem. For every input part, it predicts a rigid rotation and translation, together forming a six-degree-of-freedom pose that places the parts into a single shape.

The proposed method represents the parts and their relationships in a dynamic graph. An iterative graph neural network refines the assembly from coarse estimates toward finer arrangements. A relation reasoning module and an aggregation module update both the part features and the relationships between parts, allowing the graph representation to change as the proposed assembly develops.

This approach makes geometric reasoning and relationships among parts part of the same refinement process. The authors report extensive experiments and quantitative comparisons against three strong baseline methods that demonstrate its effectiveness. The scope is the visual prediction of assembled poses; robotic planning and control are identified as subsequent parts of an autonomous assembly system.
neurips-2020-generative-3d-part-assembly.tldr: A dynamic graph neural network iteratively predicts the rotations and positions needed to assemble 3D parts into one shape.

paragraphs: Explaining a prediction requires more than identifying influential individual inputs when their effects depend on one another. Feature interactions capture this contextual dependence: a group of features can jointly affect a prediction in a way that deserves its own explanation. This paper addresses both finding those interactions and assigning interpretable attributions to them.

The authors introduce Archipelago, a framework designed to address shortcomings of existing interaction attribution methods. Those methods may be difficult to interpret, restricted to particular models, or lack an axiomatic foundation. Archipelago brings interaction detection and attribution together while also aiming to scale to real-world settings. Its purpose is to explain how joint effects contribute to predictions, beyond merely reporting that an interaction exists.

Experiments using standard annotation labels indicate significantly more interpretable explanations than comparable approaches. The paper also provides visualizations that offer insights into deep neural networks. These results concern the usefulness of interaction-level explanations: identifying related inputs becomes more informative when the explanation also communicates their combined impact on the model’s prediction.
neurips-2020-how-does-this-interaction-a.tldr: Archipelago detects feature interactions and attributes their joint effects to make model predictions more interpretable.

paragraphs: Human gaze can provide supervision for attention mechanisms in language models, but suitable gaze datasets are scarce. This paper introduces a hybrid text saliency model that combines a cognitive model of reading with explicit supervision from human gaze. The model predicts reading durations, creating a way to carry information from observed reading behavior into language processing.

Across four corpora, the predicted durations are highly correlated with measured human gaze. The authors then introduce a joint modeling approach that integrates these saliency predictions into the attention layer of a network for a particular language task. This integration does not require human gaze measurements specific to that task, addressing the data bottleneck that motivates the work.

The joint model improves paraphrase generation on Quora Question Pairs by more than 10% in BLEU-4 over the stated state of the art. It also achieves state-of-the-art sentence compression performance on the Google Sentence Compression corpus. These results demonstrate a practical connection between cognitive reading models, gaze supervision, and task-focused neural attention.
neurips-2020-improving-natural-language-.tldr: A hybrid reading-and-gaze model guides neural attention and improves language tasks without requiring task-specific gaze data.

paragraphs: Kernel-based statistical tests can become more powerful when their hyperparameters are chosen using data. Common approaches separate the sample into a portion for tuning and a portion for testing. This makes the behavior of the test under the null hypothesis easier to handle, but leaves fewer observations for the actual test and can reduce its ability to detect a difference.

This paper proposes using the full sample for both hyperparameter learning and testing. Inspired by selective inference, the method accounts for the dependence created when the same observations serve both purposes. The authors show that the test can be correctly calibrated despite this dependence and provide a test threshold in closed form.

The approach applies to the setting of modern kernel tests such as maximum mean discrepancy and kernelized Stein discrepancy. At the same significance level, experiments show greater test power than data splitting across all split proportions considered. The result demonstrates that accounting for data reuse can preserve calibration while recovering power otherwise lost to splitting.
neurips-2020-learning-kernel-tests-witho.tldr: A selectively calibrated kernel-testing method reuses the full sample for tuning and testing, improving empirical power over data splitting.

paragraphs: This paper compares Local SGD and Minibatch SGD when different machines optimize different convex objectives and can communicate only intermittently. Each machine receives noisy gradient information about its own objective, while the shared goal is to minimize the average objective. The analysis therefore focuses on heterogeneous distributed learning, where local optimization targets need not agree.

The authors argue that even unaccelerated Minibatch SGD has guarantees that dominate all existing analyses of Local SGD in this setting. This is a comparison of theoretical guarantees, so it does not establish that Minibatch SGD wins on every individual run. They also show that accelerated Minibatch SGD is optimal when heterogeneity is high, identifying a regime where its guarantees are especially strong.

At the same time, the paper provides the first upper bound for Local SGD that improves over Minibatch SGD in a non-homogeneous regime. Together, these results make the degree of heterogeneity central to the comparison. Local SGD can have a theoretical advantage under some differing local objectives, while strong heterogeneity favors the accelerated minibatch approach.
neurips-2020-minibatch-vs-local-sgd-for-.tldr: The analysis identifies heterogeneous regimes favoring accelerated Minibatch SGD and a non-homogeneous regime where Local SGD has a better bound.

paragraphs: This paper trains a policy from datasets collected on multiple tasks so it can handle unseen tasks drawn from the same distribution. Because the new task’s identity is not supplied, the policy must infer it from transitions involving states, actions, and rewards. Task inference is therefore a central part of deciding how to act.

The authors identify a shortcut that can undermine this inference. When training datasets have very different state-action distributions, the model may associate those patterns with task identity and ignore rewards. MBML addresses this problem through metric learning with a triplet loss. To construct difficult negative examples, it approximates training-task reward functions and uses them to relabel transitions.

The method aims to make task inference more robust to misleading differences between datasets. The authors also evaluate a setting that permits further training on unseen tasks. There, initializing from the learned policy produces significantly faster convergence than random initialization, with improvements of up to 80% across five MuJoCo task distributions. That finding concerns adaptation with additional training.
neurips-2020-multi-task-batch-reinforcem.tldr: MBML uses metric learning and reward relabeling to strengthen task inference and accelerate subsequent learning on unseen tasks.

paragraphs: Different interventions in a causal system can be related even when they change different sets of variables. This paper studies how to learn those relationships jointly using the system’s directed acyclic graph. Its DAG-GP model shares information across continuous intervention choices and across experiments that intervene on different variables, rather than learning each intervention function independently.

A central challenge is that intervention functions can have input spaces of different dimensions. DAG-GP captures their correlations through a well-defined integral operator. The model accommodates different assumptions about which data are available, and the theoretical results describe when and how it can be formulated for a given causal graph. Thus, the graph helps determine the structure of information sharing.

The authors evaluate predictions and uncertainty calibration in real and synthetic settings. DAG-GP achieves the best fitting performance relative to the single-task models compared. When incorporated into sequential decision frameworks such as active learning or Bayesian optimization, it also helps select optimal interventions faster than competing approaches, connecting shared causal learning with more efficient experimental choices.
neurips-2020-multi-task-causal-learning-.tldr: DAG-GP shares information among related causal interventions to improve predictions and speed intervention selection in the evaluated settings.

paragraphs: Different kinds of data often describe the same underlying phenomenon. A multimodal generative model needs to learn both the distribution of those observations and the dependencies among their modalities. This paper targets the difficulty and inefficiency of training existing models that use a multimodal evidence lower bound, or ELBO, as their learning objective.

The authors propose a new objective based on Jensen-Shannon divergence for multiple distributions. It uses a dynamic prior to approximate both unimodal posteriors, based on individual modalities, and a joint posterior, based on modalities together. Handling these approximations simultaneously gives the training objective a direct role in connecting separate information sources with their combined representation.

The paper proves that the resulting multimodal Jensen-Shannon divergence objective, called mmJSD, optimizes an ELBO. This supplies a theoretical foundation alongside the proposed efficiency benefit. Extensive experiments report advantages over previous work on unsupervised generative learning tasks. The findings support the objective as a useful way to train multimodal models while retaining an established lower-bound formulation.
neurips-2020-multimodal-generative-learn.tldr: mmJSD uses a dynamic prior and multimodal Jensen-Shannon divergence to train generative models with a proven ELBO objective.

paragraphs: REVEL addresses safe exploration in reinforcement learning with continuous states and actions. The computational obstacle is that repeatedly verifying neural networks during learning is infeasible. The framework uses two policy classes to make progress: a flexible neurosymbolic class with approximate gradients and a more restricted symbolic class that supports efficient verification.

Learning proceeds through a mirror-descent process over policies. Each iteration safely moves a symbolic policy into the neurosymbolic space, applies safe gradient updates, and projects the result back into the safe symbolic subset. This sequence provides a way to use neural policy updates while maintaining the framework’s safety guarantee without explicitly verifying the neural networks themselves.

In the reported experiments, REVEL enforces safe exploration in many scenarios where Constrained Policy Optimization does not. It can also find policies that outperform those produced by earlier verified-exploration approaches. The contribution joins a formally grounded learning procedure with empirical evidence that the symbolic restrictions can coexist with useful policy improvement in the continuous settings studied.
neurips-2020-neurosymbolic-reinforcement.tldr: REVEL combines neural policy updates with verifiable symbolic policies to enable provably safe exploration without repeated neural-network verification.

paragraphs: This paper asks how the internal structure of a neural representation affects resistance to perturbations. It connects observations from mouse visual cortex with artificial neural networks, focusing on a covariance spectrum that follows a 1/n pattern. The spectrum describes how variation is distributed across the representation, making it a structural property of the neural code.

The authors use adversarial robustness to investigate a theory about the causal role of that spectral pattern. They impose the experimentally observed structure on artificial networks and examine the resulting benefits empirically. They also study its role in multilayer architectures, bringing attention to the representations formed inside the network as computation passes through successive layers.

The reported results show increased resistance to adversarial attacks when this structure is imposed. These findings provide empirical support for a connection between representation structure and robustness in the tested artificial networks. They also complement theory linking wide neural networks with kernel methods by highlighting the role of intermediate representations, rather than considering only the network’s overall input-output relationship.
neurips-2020-on-1-n-neural-representatio.tldr: Imposing a covariance-spectrum pattern observed in mouse visual cortex improves adversarial robustness in the artificial networks studied.

paragraphs: Dense neural probes can contain more electrode sites than available recording channels. For example, the Neuropixels probe described here has 960 addressable electrodes and 384 channels. Choosing which electrodes to record therefore affects how many neurons can be distinguished. This paper introduces classification-based selection, or CBS, to adapt those choices using recorded neural data.

CBS jointly optimizes electrode selections across all recording channels to improve the isolation quality of detected neurons. In non-human-primate Neuropixels experiments, it yields a neuron count similar to what would be obtained by recording every electrode simultaneously. Counts improve by 41–85% over previously published electrode-selection strategies, and selected electrodes have higher average signal-to-noise ratio per channel.

Using spike timing, the isolated neurons show a 73% match to the complete set of recordable neurons near the probe. This result describes which neurons are recovered, complementing the overall count comparison. The work suggests adaptive selection could help neurotechnologies use limited recording bandwidth more effectively, especially as bandwidth becomes increasingly restrictive.
neurips-2020-optimal-adaptive-electrode-.tldr: CBS adapts electrode selection to recover more isolated neurons from a limited number of recording channels.

paragraphs: This paper predicts how many optimization steps a pretrained deep network will need to reach a chosen loss during fine-tuning. Its starting point is that fine-tuning dynamics can be well approximated by a linearized model. The method uses that approximation to forecast progress without carrying out the actual training process.

The authors solve a low-dimensional stochastic differential equation in function space to approximate loss and accuracy along the training trajectory. From that trajectory, they estimate when stochastic gradient descent will reach the target loss. The prediction therefore concerns training progress measured in optimization steps, with the linearized dynamics providing the basis for the estimate.

In experiments involving a ResNet across multiple datasets and hyperparameters, predictions fall within a 20% error margin while costing 30–45 times less than actual training. The authors also study computational and memory reductions. In particular, spectral properties of the gradient matrix allow prediction on a large dataset while processing only a subset of its samples, reducing the data processing needed for the forecast.
neurips-2020-predicting-training-time-wi.tldr: A linearized model of fine-tuning predicts steps to a target loss at substantially lower cost than training in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper develops an efficient way to evaluate the proximity operator of the matrix perspective function. The function is jointly convex over a vector and a compatible symmetric matrix. A proximity operator supplies an optimization building block, so making this operator tractable can support larger statistical estimation problems that involve the same mathematical structure.

The main result gives an almost closed-form expression: the remaining implicit calculation is a semismooth root-finding problem in one variable. By connecting this calculation to a matrix nearness problem, the authors derive a Newton algorithm with quadratic convergence. This reduces the unresolved part of the operator evaluation to a focused numerical procedure.

Experiments require at most eight Newton steps, with 2000-by-2000 matrices processed in under five seconds on a standard laptop. These are reported experimental results, alongside the convergence analysis. The authors then use the routine for constrained Gaussian mean and covariance estimation, graphical model selection based on pseudolikelihood, and a matrix version of scaled lasso, demonstrating its value across several optimization applications.
neurips-2020-proximity-operator-of-the-m.tldr: An almost closed-form proximity operator reduces matrix-perspective optimization to a one-variable problem solved by a quadratically convergent Newton method.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether highly sparse, trainable subnetworks can be identified at initialization without training the network or examining training data. Such pruning could reduce resource demands, but existing initialization-based methods face layer collapse: removing an entire layer too early can make the remaining network untrainable. Understanding that failure is central to the proposed solution.

The authors formulate and experimentally verify a conservation law explaining layer collapse in existing gradient-based pruning methods. The theory also shows how collapse can be avoided and motivates Iterative Synaptic Flow Pruning, or SynFlow. The algorithm can be understood as preserving total synaptic-strength flow through the initialized network while satisfying a sparsity constraint, without referring to training data.

Across VGG and ResNet models, CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny ImageNet datasets, and sparsity levels reaching 99.99%, SynFlow consistently competes with or outperforms the initialization-pruning methods compared. The findings show that data are not always required to identify useful sparse structures at initialization. The resulting subnetworks remain intended for training; it is their selection that avoids training and data.
neurips-2020-pruning-neural-networks-wit.tldr: SynFlow identifies sparse trainable subnetworks at initialization without data by preserving synaptic flow and avoiding layer collapse.

paragraphs: Value function approximation is widely successful in reinforcement learning, but theoretical understanding has been stronger for linear approximations than for general function classes. This paper establishes a provably efficient algorithm for general value function approximation, extending the theory beyond the linear setting. Its guarantee depends on whether the value functions admit approximation within a specified function class.

The regret bound grows roughly with the square root of the number of environment interactions, multiplied by a polynomial in the planning horizon and a function-class complexity measure, with logarithmic factors suppressed. That complexity measure depends on eluder dimension and log-covering numbers. Consequently, the guarantee makes the approximation class’s complexity an explicit part of how difficult learning is.

The theory generalizes the linear Markov decision process assumption to broader function classes. The algorithm is also model-free, addressing learning through value approximation without requiring a learned environment model. The result supplies a framework for understanding the effectiveness of practical algorithms, while keeping its efficiency claim tied to the stated approximation and complexity conditions.
neurips-2020-reinforcement-learning-with.tldr: A model-free algorithm obtains regret guarantees for general value-function classes under approximation and bounded-complexity conditions.

paragraphs: Numerical solvers approximate partial differential equations, and discretization can leave effects unresolved. Machine learning can help by predicting corrections, but those corrections also change the states encountered in later solver steps. This paper studies how to train correction functions for iterative solvers so that the learned model experiences the consequences of its own earlier corrections.

The proposed approach includes the solver inside the training loop through differentiable physics. The model interacts with the evolving simulation during training, receiving inputs that reflect previous corrections. This matters because learning a correction for one state is only part of the task: the correction must also work as the solver repeatedly produces new states.

The authors find that solver-integrated training significantly outperforms previously used approaches and even tailored supervised variants. They report improved accuracy with stable rollouts lasting several hundred recurrent evaluation steps. Evaluations cover equations ranging from nonlinear advection-diffusion systems to three-dimensional Navier-Stokes flows, supporting the approach across the varied physical systems tested.
neurips-2020-solver-in-the-loop-learning.tldr: Training correction models inside differentiable PDE solvers improves accuracy and supports stable multistep simulations in the evaluated systems.

paragraphs: Quasi-Monte Carlo methods use constructed point sets for tasks such as approximating integrals and sampling in scientific computation. Rank-1 lattices are attractive because their construction and operation are simple once a generating vector is available. Finding that vector, however, can require a time-consuming exhaustive search. This paper proposes a closed-form construction based on group theory.

The construction reduces the number of distinct distances between pairs of points to produce a more regular lattice. The authors also prove lower and upper bounds on the minimum pairwise distance for any non-degenerate rank-1 lattice. These theoretical results characterize an important geometric property of the point sets, alongside the practical method for constructing them.

Empirically, the proposed methods produce near-optimal lattices relative to Korobov exhaustive search when judged by minimum distance in the l1 and l2 norms. Experiments also show superior approximation performance on benchmark integration and kernel approximation problems. The contribution links a simpler construction procedure with favorable geometry and demonstrated approximation quality in the tested problems.
neurips-2020-subgroup-based-rank-1-latti.tldr: A group-theoretic closed-form construction produces rank-1 lattices with near-optimal empirical spacing and strong approximation performance.

paragraphs: Active learning lets a learner adaptively choose which examples to label, aiming to reduce expensive supervision. Yet prior results show that this flexibility alone need not improve sample complexity for important classes such as linear separators. This paper studies how the picture changes when the learner can also ask comparison queries under weak distributional assumptions.

With those additions, the authors show that active learning can require exponentially fewer samples. The conditions are part of the result: the improvement comes from combining comparison queries with the stated assumptions about the data distribution. The work therefore identifies additional information that can make adaptive learning substantially more efficient than label queries alone.

The results also extend to Reliable and Probably Useful learning, where the learner may abstain but is not allowed to make mistakes. Earlier label-query results made this requirement prohibitively expensive in sample complexity. With comparisons, the paper shows that this stronger learning requirement costs at most an additional logarithmic factor in both passive and active regimes, making abstention-compatible reliability much more accessible theoretically.
neurips-2020-the-power-of-comparisons-fo.tldr: Under weak distributional assumptions, comparison queries enable exponential active-learning savings and efficient learning with reliable abstention.

paragraphs: Consistency training uses unlabeled examples by encouraging a model to make stable predictions when its inputs are perturbed. This paper argues that the quality of those perturbations is crucial. It replaces simple noise with stronger data augmentation methods, including RandAugment and back-translation, while retaining the same overall consistency-training framework.

The method brings substantial improvements across six language tasks and three vision tasks. On IMDb, it achieves an error rate of 4.20 with only 20 labeled examples, outperforming the stated state-of-the-art model trained with 25,000 labels. On CIFAR-10, it reports an error rate of 5.43 using 250 labeled examples and outperforms the prior approaches considered.

The authors also show that the approach combines well with transfer learning, including BERT fine-tuning. Benefits extend to ImageNet both with 10% labeled data and with the full labeled set plus 1.3 million additional unlabeled examples. These findings make augmentation quality a practical design choice for extracting value from unlabeled data, across both scarce-label and larger-data settings.
neurips-2020-unsupervised-data-augmentat.tldr: Stronger augmentation improves consistency training, producing substantial gains from unlabeled data across language and vision tasks.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows are generative models that support efficient sampling and fast density computation, but training them on complex images can be expensive. This paper introduces Wavelet Flow to reduce that cost and make higher-resolution modeling practical. Its architecture uses wavelets to organize the generative model around explicit signal scales.

The multiscale representation naturally includes models for lower-resolution signals and conditional generation of higher-resolution signals. This gives the architecture a built-in connection to super resolution: higher-resolution content is modeled in relation to lower-resolution content. Scale is therefore an explicit part of the model’s organization, tying together coarse signals and their finer detail.

The authors demonstrate generative modeling of high-resolution data, including 1024-by-1024 images, described as impractical for previous models. On standard low-resolution benchmarks, Wavelet Flow remains competitive with earlier normalizing flows in bits per dimension while training up to 15 times faster. The results support its combination of reduced training cost and competitive density modeling in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2020-wavelet-flow-fast-training-.tldr: Wavelet Flow explicitly models image scales to enable high-resolution generation and up to 15-fold faster training.
